description: One variety of one crop: what it is grafted on, who pollinates it, what it yields and how long it takes to get there. EVERY RULE ABOUT A VARIETY IS A RULE ABOUT ITS CROP — whether the name is unique, whether `maturity_years` is meaningful at all — so the checking lives in `crop.py`, where the whole list and the growth cycle are in hand. There is nothing true of one of these rows on its own.

fields.description: The cultivar as it is sold and as the block is known by — 'Bing', 'Rainier', 'Honeycrisp'. UNIQUE WITHIN THE CROP, enforced by the parent: two rows called 'Bing' are two rows about one tree, and every read that groups a packout or a yield by variety would count it twice.
fields.label: Variety

fields.description:
What this variety is USUALLY grafted onto in this operation — 'Gisela 6', 'Mazzard', 'M.9'. THE ROOTSTOCK IS HALF THE TREE and it decides what the scion does not: vigour, final size, planting density, how soon it bears and how it takes wet ground.

THIS COLUMN IS NOT THE BINDING ANSWER AND MUST NOT BE READ AS ONE. A crop's variety list is a catalogue, and a catalogue has one row per variety — so this can hold exactly one rootstock for 'Bing', while the actual farm has Bing on Mazzard in the old block and Bing on Gisela 6 in the 2019 planting. Those are different trees with different vigour, different density and different yields, and a per-acre figure quoted against the wrong one is not comparable to anything.

THE BINDING ROOTSTOCK IS ON THE PLANTING: `Planting Season.rootstock` for a block-year, and `Field.rootstock` for the block itself. Both predate this note and both are where a reader should look. What is left here is a default for the case where a planting records none — v0.114.0 backfilled this value down onto every planting that had a blank, so on a migrated site the plantings already carry their own answer and this column is only ever the seed for the next one.
fields.label: Typical Rootstock (catalogue default)

fields.description: The cross-incompatibility group, for the varieties that have one — cherries are 'S1S2', 'S3S4' and so on, apples are numbered bloom groups. WHAT IT IS FOR IS THE ONE QUESTION A BLOCK PLAN CANNOT GET WRONG TWICE: two varieties in the same incompatibility group will not set fruit for each other, and the block finds out four years later. Free text rather than a Select because the notation differs by species and a list would refuse the next one.
fields.label: Pollination Group

fields.description: What a mature acre of it is expected to give, in the unit the operation counts that crop in — tons for cherries, bins for apples. THE UNIT IS NOT STORED HERE ON PURPOSE: it is the crop's own harvest unit, and a per-row unit would let one crop's varieties be quoted in three of them and silently summed. An expectation, not a record — what actually came off is a Scale Ticket.
fields.label: Expected Yield / Acre

fields.description: Years from planting to the first commercial crop. MEANINGFUL ONLY ON A PERENNIAL, and refused outright on an Annual or Biennial crop by the parent — an annual that takes four years to bear is a contradiction, not a long-lived one. What it is really for is capitalisation: the non-bearing years are development cost carried into the orchard's basis rather than expensed against a season that produced nothing, and this is the column that says how many of them there are.
fields.label: Years to Maturity

fields.description: This variety's own pick Brix, where it departs from the crop's. SPARSE AND PER FIELD, the same shape as the water overlay beside it: a blank cell is a variety with no opinion and the crop's figure stands. A ZERO IS NOT A BLANK — it is a claim that this variety is picked at zero Brix, which is why the resolver distinguishes the two rather than reading `float(value or 0)`.
fields.label: Target Brix

name: Crop Variety
